newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission proposes better deal for part-time work.
newsitem.headline: Commission proposes better deal for part-time work.

text.p: The European Commission proposed rules on Wednesday which would guarantee part-time workers the same rights as full-time colleagues in a move to encourage more people to take up part-time jobs.

The planned rules are based on an agreement finalised on June 6 by labour and employers' groups -- the EU employers' confederation UNICE, the trade union group ETUC and the public employers group CEEP -- after a year of negotiations.
The EU executive intends to put the seven-point binding directive to EU social affairs ministers on October 7.
It gives the EU's 15 member states two years to remove discrimination against workers on part-time contracts in order to encourage more people to take up such flexible types of work.
The rules obliges employers to offer part-time workers the same employment conditions as full-timers and prevents them from sacking full-timers who refuse to switch to part-time work.
EU governments will be forced to introduce effective penalites to deter companies from breaking the rules, the Commission said.

The rules do not cover people doing other atypical types of work, such as temporary or seasonal jobs, or working from home, but labour and employers have recognised the need to broker a similar arrangement for these people.
They will not apply to casual workers either in member states which can provide "objective reasons" for not giving these workers the same social protection as full-time employees.
The Commission said EU governments could, if they wanted, bring in even stricter standards but they could not use the new directive to justify a cut in existing levels of worker protection.

The trades unions and employers' groups -- the so-called social partners -- agreed in June 1996 to open talks on rights for part-time workers after the Commission asked them to consider ways of ensuring that employees in a broad range of flexible jobs did not face discrimination.

The directive is the second piece of legislation to be worked out under the Maastricht Treaty's social protocol, which gives the social partners the right to strike a deal and then ask the Council of Ministers to turn it into EU law.
The British Labour government's decision to sign up to the social chapter means that British workers will be covered by the new rules in the same way as workers in other parts of the EU.
